main.title: Crash Twinsanity
main.summary: Crash's worst enemy becomes his most awkward piece of equipment in a journey through connected comic set pieces.

cards.heading: The game
cards.text: Crash Twinsanity is a 2004 platform adventure by Traveller's Tales Oxford Studio for PlayStation 2 and Xbox. An attack by the Evil Twins forces Crash and Cortex into an uneasy partnership. Connected areas carry the pair between platforming, arguments and elaborate accidents, accompanied by Spiralmouth's vocal soundtrack.

cards.heading: An enemy within reach
cards.text: Crash can grab Cortex by the ankles and swing him as a weapon. The doctor's body reaches enemies and objects differently from an ordinary spin, turning the partnership into a practical change in the controls. Elsewhere Cortex must be thrown towards a place Crash cannot reach directly. A story about two enemies cooperating is therefore acted out through the player: progress means finding a use for a companion who would usually be the target at the end of the level.

cards.heading: Keep the pair moving
cards.text: The pair also gets caught in movements that neither character can easily stop. Locked together in a rolling fight, they become a ball that the player steers around obstacles. On slippery slopes, Cortex serves as an unwilling board beneath Crash. Direction and momentum take over from the usual sequence of jumps, while the characters keep quarrelling inside the action. These passages carry the comedy through the controls, making a dangerous descent and an argument between partners happen at the same time.

cards.heading: Another character, another route
cards.text: Control eventually passes to Cortex and to his niece Nina, each bringing another way through the scenery. Cortex's ray gun shifts attention towards targets and ammunition, while Nina's mechanical arms let her reach particular holds and cross gaps. Optional gems encourage a closer look around these spaces and unlock concept artwork. Their placement gives an extra purpose to the different abilities: following the main route advances the partnership, while a difficult side jump can reward someone who has learned how the current character moves.

main.title: Mortal Kombat: Deception
main.summary: Mortal Kombat: Deception is a 2004 fighting game developed and published by Midway.

cards.text: Mortal Kombat: Deception is a 2004 fighting game developed and published by Midway. The sixth main installment in the Mortal Kombat franchise and sequel to Mortal Kombat: Deadly Alliance (2002), it was released for the PlayStation 2 (PS2) and Xbox in October 2004, the GameCube in March 2005, and for the PlayStation Portable (PSP) as Mortal Kombat: Unchained in November 2006. Following on from the events of Deadly Alliance, the game’s plot centers on the recently revived Dragon King Onaga, who upon defeating the Thunder God Raiden and sorcerers Quan Chi and Shang Tsung attempts to conquer various realms, meanwhile surviving warriors from prior MK titles join forces in a bid to stop him. In addition to online play and new chess and puzzle minigames, a revamped Konquest Mode from Deadly Alliance features a secondary plot line following the life of Shujinko, a warrior deceived by Onaga into finding artifacts to increase his power.

Designed by series co-creator Ed Boon, the game was created with the intent of surprising MK fans with new and returning content, as well as providing a more realistic combat experience in order to preserve the series signature gory violence. Several parts of the gameplay, such as combos and arenas, were redesigned to accommodate the new style of realism as well as be more interactive for players. In addition, the game was designed with the online play in mind, which had yet to be established into a fighting game.

Upon release, Deception was positively received by critics, who praised the reworked combat and plethora of new features, but criticized the revamped Konquest Mode due to its poor story and voice acting. The game managed to sell more than 1 million units by the end of 2005 and was nominated as the best fighting game of 2004 by several game publications. It has since been regarded as having been the first fighting game to incorporate online multiplayer, which later became an industry standard for the genre moving forward. A sequel to Deception, Mortal Kombat Armageddon, was released in 2006.

main.title: Fire Emblem: The Sacred Stones
main.summary: Fire Emblem: The Sacred Stones is a tactical role-playing game developed by Intelligent Systems, and published by Nintendo for the Game Boy Advance handheld video game console in 2004 for Japan and 2005 in the West.

cards.text: Fire Emblem: The Sacred Stones is a tactical role-playing game developed by Intelligent Systems, and published by Nintendo for the Game Boy Advance handheld video game console in 2004 for Japan and 2005 in the West. It is the eighth entry in the Fire Emblem series, the second to be released outside Japan, and the third and final title to be developed for the Game Boy Advance after The Binding Blade and its prequel The Blazing Blade.

Set in a separate continuity to earlier Fire Emblem titles, The Sacred Stones takes place on the fictional continent of Magvel, which is divided into six nations, built around five magical stones said to be linked to the imprisonment of an ancient demon. When one of the six nations, the Grado Empire, invades its neighbors and begins destroying the stones, protagonists Eirika and Ephraim of the royal family of Renais set out to gather allies and halt Grado's conquest, while also trying to uncover the reasons for the war. The gameplay is similar to previous Fire Emblem games, focusing on turn-based, tactical movement of units across a grid-based battlefield. Core features of the game include permanent death for characters defeated in battle and support conversations that grant advantages to certain units in battle.

The Sacred Stones began development alongside Fire Emblem: Path of Radiance as a side project, sharing much of its visual design and mechanics with The Blazing Blade while incorporating elements from earlier entries such as Fire Emblem Gaiden. First announced in mid-2004, it was heavily promoted in Japan. When released, it sold over 230,000 units during 2004, with a further 90,000 being sold upon its North American debut. Reception was positive overall for its story, characters and gameplay, although many critics cited it as being too similar to its predecessor. The Sacred Stones would be the last original handheld Fire Emblem title until Fire Emblem Awakening for the Nintendo 3DS in 2012.

main.title: Paper Mario: The Thousand-Year Door
main.subtitle: Paper transformations and a battle stage
main.summary: On October 11, 2004, Paper Mario: The Thousand-Year Door arrived on Nintendo GameCube in North America, after its Japanese release on July 22; Europe would receive it on November 12.

cards.heading: Paper transformations and a battle stage
cards.text: Paper Mario: The Thousand-Year Door reached GameCube in Japan on July 22, 2004, North America on October 11 and Europe on November 12. Intelligent Systems expands the Nintendo 64 RPG's paper identity through transformations: Mario can fold into an airplane or slip through narrow openings. Battles take place on a stage, with partners, badges and an audience adding choices and surprises to its turn-based encounters.

cards.heading: The audience joins the battle
cards.text: Timed commands ask the player to perform an action as well as choose it. The watching audience reacts, contributes to resources and can disrupt a battle, while scenery supplies further unexpected events. Treating an encounter as a performance gives its rules a visible setting and connects execution to the reaction from the seats.

cards.heading: Folding opens a route
cards.text: Paper transformations turn narrow gaps and open spaces into different kinds of routes. An opening can admit a folded Mario, while an airplane form crosses distances. His appearance therefore suggests actions the player can learn to recognise in the scenery. New transformations encourage revisiting obstacles with a different way through them.

cards.heading: Partners bring abilities and stories
cards.text: Goombella, Koops and other companions introduce personal stories as they join the journey. Their abilities also affect exploration and combat, connecting characterisation to practical uses. Familiar Mushroom Kingdom species acquire individual voices and ambitions, allowing the writing to develop a varied travelling party from recognisable figures.

cards.heading: Choosing badges for the next encounter
cards.text: A limited pool of badge points determines which combat advantages can be equipped. Badges change attacks, defence, risk and the usefulness of particular actions. Preparing a setup supplies the options brought into battle; timed commands then affect their execution. Those two kinds of decision give players room to vary a strategy within the clear turn-based structure.

main.title: WarioWare: Twisted!
main.summary: WarioWare: Twisted! is an action video game developed by Nintendo and Intelligent Systems and published by Nintendo for the Game Boy Advance.

cards.text: WarioWare: Twisted! is an action video game developed by Nintendo and Intelligent Systems and published by Nintendo for the Game Boy Advance. It was released on October 14, 2004 in Japan; May 19, 2005 in Australia; and May 23, 2005 in North America. The third game in the WarioWare series and the seventh in the Wario series overall, Twisted! was the last Wario game to be released on a Game Boy family system, having been released after the launch of the Nintendo DS outside of Japan.

Wario and his friend Dr. Crygor invent Game Boy Advance games and units that only react when tilted around. The game follows the WarioWare formula with a variety of games that last for only a few seconds. The cartridge utilizes a gyro sensor and players must spin and twist in order to play the games.
Twisted! was critically acclaimed and has won numerous awards. Reviewers found the gyro sensor to be innovative and adding to the gameplay aspect.
It is one of only two Game Boy Advance games to include force feedback, the other being Drill Dozer.

main.title: F-Zero Climax
main.subtitle: The portable circuit gains a workshop
main.summary: F-Zero Climax is Suzak's Japan-released Game Boy Advance racing game continuing the fast machines and animated-series connections of GP Legend. Grand Prix events, time trials and Survival challenges provide different ways to test control on its courses. A track editor adds another role for the player, allowing the racing problems to be designed as well as solved. The collection keeps the familiar view of a vehicle racing over a scrolling course, while the new creation tools make its corners and hazards something that can be deliberately arranged for another driver to confront.

cards.heading: The portable circuit gains a workshop
cards.text: F-Zero Climax is Suzak's Japan-released Game Boy Advance racing game continuing the fast machines and animated-series connections of GP Legend. Grand Prix events, time trials and Survival challenges provide different ways to test control on its courses. A track editor adds another role for the player, allowing the racing problems to be designed as well as solved. The collection keeps the familiar view of a vehicle racing over a scrolling course, while the new creation tools make its corners and hazards something that can be deliberately arranged for another driver to confront.

cards.heading: A short test can isolate a difficult skill
cards.text: Survival challenges alter the conditions of a race, asking the player to handle situations such as reduced health or a short course without protective barriers. Zero Test offers time trials built around small sections rather than a complete championship event. These modes concentrate attention on the control needed in a particular circumstance. A fast approach may be useful until braking becomes essential to remain on the track at the finish. The smaller tests make success depend on reading the objective carefully instead of assuming that every event rewards the highest possible speed throughout.

cards.heading: Build the corner that another racer must learn
cards.text: Edit mode assembles tracks from pieces of different shapes and sizes, with obstacles selected for the resulting sections. A limited construction budget gives those choices a practical constraint, requiring the player to decide which parts of a proposed route deserve the available space. The finished course can then be approached as a racing problem. The tool reverses the usual relationship with an F-Zero track: a corner that once demanded practice becomes something placed deliberately, allowing its creator to discover how an arrangement of straights, turns and hazards actually feels when driven at speed.

main.title: Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas
main.summary: Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas is a 2004 action-adventure game developed by Rockstar North and published by Rockstar Games.

cards.heading: CJ returns to a changing home
cards.text: Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas is a 2004 action-adventure game developed by Rockstar North and published by Rockstar Games. It is the fifth main game in the Grand Theft Auto series and the seventh overall entry, following 2002's Grand Theft Auto: Vice City. Set within the fictional U.S. state of San Andreas (based on California and Nevada) in 1992, the game follows Carl "CJ" Johnson, a former gangster who returns home following his mother's murder. Finding his old street gang in decline, CJ works to rebuild it while clashing with corrupt authorities and rival criminals, and gradually uncovers the truth behind his mother's death.

cards.heading: Researching three cities and their cultures
cards.text: The game is played from a third-person perspective and its world is navigated on foot or by vehicle. The open world design lets the player freely roam San Andreas, consisting of three major metropolitan cities: Los Santos, San Fierro, and Las Venturas, based on Los Angeles, San Francisco, and Las Vegas, respectively. Rockstar conducted on-site research in each city and consulted Los Angeles natives DJ Pooh, Estevan Oriol, and Mister Cartoon for help imitating the city's culture. The narrative is based on multiple real-life events in Los Angeles, including the Bloods and Crips street gang rivalry, the 1990s crack epidemic, the 1992 Los Angeles riots, and the Rampart scandal. The 75-person development team spent nearly two years creating the game. San Andreas was released in October 2004 for the PlayStation 2.

cards.heading: A large audience and a ratings controversy
cards.text: The game received critical acclaim for its characters, narrative, open world design, and visual fidelity, but mixed responses towards its mission design, technical issues, and portrayal of race. It generated controversy when the hidden "Hot Coffee" sex minigame was discovered, briefly requiring the game to be re-rated Adults Only. San Andreas received year-end accolades from several gaming publications, and it is considered one of the sixth generation of console gaming's most significant titles and among the best video games ever made. It was released for Windows and the Xbox in 2005, followed by enhanced versions and mobile ports in the 2010s, and a remastered version in 2021. San Andreas is the best-selling PlayStation 2 game with over 17.3 million copies sold, and one of the best-selling games of all time with 27.5 million copies sold overall. Its successor, Grand Theft Auto IV, was released in April 2008.

cards.heading: Three cities on one map
cards.text: Rockstar first considered three separate maps linked by public transport, then joined them with countryside and desert. Los Santos, San Fierro and Las Venturas drew on Los Angeles, San Francisco and Las Vegas. Research trips and thousands of photographs helped the artists give each city a particular character, with some images becoming textures. The resulting thirty-six-square-kilometre world was several times larger than the earlier games. Its distances made travelling between places part of the experience rather than merely changing the scenery around another city mission.

main.title: Ratchet & Clank: Up Your Arsenal
main.subtitle: An arsenal that grows with its owner
main.summary: Ratchet & Clank: Up Your Arsenal is Insomniac Games' third Ratchet & Clank adventure, released for PlayStation 2 in 2004. Ratchet and his robot companion face Dr. Nefarious, whose campaign threatens organic life across the galaxy. Planetary missions build on the series' weapons and gadgets, while a new multiplayer mode brings its combat online.

cards.heading: The galaxy calls again
cards.text: Ratchet & Clank: Up Your Arsenal is Insomniac Games' third Ratchet & Clank adventure, released for PlayStation 2 in 2004. Ratchet and his robot companion face Dr. Nefarious, whose campaign threatens organic life across the galaxy. Planetary missions build on the series' weapons and gadgets, while a new multiplayer mode brings its combat online.

cards.heading: Keeping an enemy in sight
cards.text: Strafing lets Ratchet move sideways while keeping his weapon pointed towards a target. Choosing a weapon from the quick-select menu then changes the shape of a fight: a close group calls for a different attack from an enemy across an open platform. Bolts gathered along the way pay for equipment and ammunition.

cards.heading: Weapons worth using
cards.text: Weapons gain experience through use and develop into stronger versions. Many have five upgrade levels during the first playthrough, giving a reason to bring a new purchase into combat. Ratchet's Nanotech health also grows with experience. Progress therefore changes both the tools available and the amount of punishment the player can survive.

cards.heading: A different-sized hero
cards.text: Clank's sections alter the pace and scale of the journey. He can direct small robotic helpers, while Giant Clank takes the action into much larger battles. Captain Qwark's playable Vid-Comics provide another diversion, retelling his adventures as side-scrolling stages. These interludes give the supporting cast its own part in the action.

main.title: Spyro: A Hero's Tail
main.summary: Dark Gems change the landscape around them; destroying one restores a route through a world shared by Spyro and his friends.

cards.heading: The game
cards.text: Spyro: A Hero's Tail is Eurocom's 2004 platform adventure for PlayStation 2, Xbox and GameCube. The dragon Red spreads Dark Gems through the Dragon Realms, and Spyro sets out to destroy them. Larger connected areas combine collecting and new abilities with playable sections for returning friends and Blink the mole.

cards.heading: Break the thing changing the landscape
cards.text: A Dark Gem makes its effect visible in the scenery around it. Destroying the stone restores that part of the realm and can open the way onwards. Light Gems serve another purpose, powering the Professor's machinery, while dragon eggs unlock additional features. Those separate rewards give exploration several goals at once. A visible route may depend on removing corruption, using a newly learned move or bringing back enough of the right collectible to operate a machine.

cards.heading: A breath for the obstacle ahead
cards.text: Different breaths and physical moves make the objects in a room worth inspecting. A Horn Dive breaks a chest from above, while a stronger container can require a Super Charge or a nearby firecracker. Moneybags sells lock picks for locked chests, adding a reason to decide how collected gems are spent. The next reward may therefore involve reading the obstacle before attacking it: its appearance suggests which move or purchase will turn it into something Spyro can open.

cards.heading: A friend takes another route
cards.text: Hunter's bow, Sgt. Byrd's flight and Blink's underground work give the adventure other ways to move and fight. These sections narrow attention to a different set of abilities before returning control to Spyro. The change also gives his friends practical roles in the search. A ledge, an enemy or a passage can become another kind of problem when a different character takes over, extending the journey through tasks that Spyro's usual combination of gliding, charging and breathing fire would handle differently.

main.title: Golden Joystick Awards 2004
main.summary: The Golden Joystick Awards, with every category winner of the 2004 edition.

cards.heading: The players' awards
cards.text: The Golden Joystick Awards celebrate games through a public vote, bringing players into the choice of each year's winners. The awards began in Britain with the 1983 season and later reached an international audience through online voting. Their changing categories trace the growth of games: home computers and consoles, handhelds, online play, independent studios, performance and music. Alongside the public vote, special honours recognise individual contributions to the industry. Each edition preserves its own category names, so the results also show what players and the awards organisers considered worth celebrating at the time.
